extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and graduate students in psychology (humor, personality, affective science)
extracted.subtask_description: Define and measure temperamental dispositions underlying humor (cheerfulness, seriousness, bad mood) as states and traits; provide facets, measurement (STCI), hypothesized relationships to humor behavior, and methodological guidance for experimental and correlational work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperamental basis of humor: cheerfulness, seriousness, bad mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheerfulness, seriousness, and bad mood as traits form the temperamental basis of humor; as states they represent intrapersonally varying dispositions for humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The model assumes humor is multidimensional and bipolar (humorfulness and humorlessness), covers affective and mental factors, and that these three constructs (as states and traits) are the core temperamental dimensions to specify and measure when studying individual differences in humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: State–trait distinction for humor dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between actual (state) dispositions and habitual (trait) dispositions for cheerfulness, seriousness, and bad mood; the same concepts are used for both levels to study homologous relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States are transient, stimulus-dependent, and have timing (onset, apex, offset); traits represent prevalence, typical intensity, duration, and robustness across situations. Use both state and trait measures to examine convergence and moderating effects (e.g., traits as moderators of situational effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhilaration (amusement) as core affective response
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhilaration is the emotion/process of becoming cheerful (temporary rise in cheerfulness) with behavioral, physiological, and experiential components and specific 'exhilarants' (e.g., humor, tickling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat exhilaration as distinct from more tonic cheerfulness: it is brief, has a pronounced apex, and is stimulus-timed. Use measures of facial/display behavior, experience, and physiology to assess exhilaration as an outcome of humor stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait cheerfulness (STCI-T facets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trait cheerfulness is operationalized with five facets (CH1–CH5): prevalence of cheerful mood; low threshold for smiling and laughter; composed view of adverse life circumstances; broad range of active elicitors of cheerfulness and smiling/laughter; generally cheerful interaction style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trait cheerfulness is unipolar; high scorers are predicted to have lower thresholds for entering cheerful states, greater intensity/duration of exhilaration, higher smiling/laughter, and greater tendency to initiate/entertain in social situations. The 'cheerful composure' facet (CH3) is emphasized as predicting robustness under adversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait seriousness (STCI-T facets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trait seriousness is operationalized with six facets (SE1–SE6): prevalence of serious states; perceiving everyday happenings as important and considering them thoroughly; tendency to plan ahead and set long-range goals; preference for activities with concrete, rational reasons; preference for sober, object-oriented communication; humorless attitude about cheerfulness-related behavior, persons, stimuli, situations, and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seriousness is conceptualized as a mental/frame-of-mind axis linked to reduced interest in playful/humorous interaction and to specific humor preferences (e.g., sensitivity to truth/message). It may correlate with lower playfulness and certain cognitive/attitudinal aspects of humor creation and appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait bad mood (STCI-T facets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trait bad mood is operationalized with five facets (BM1–BM5): prevalence of bad mood; prevalence of sadness (despondent/distressed mood); sad behavior in cheerfulness-evoking situations and attitudes toward such situations; prevalence of ill-humored (sullen, grumpy) feelings; ill-humored behavior in cheerfulness-evoking situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad mood is an affective form of humorlessness distinct from seriousness. It predicts susceptibility to negative affect, may hinder induction of cheerfulness/exhilaration, and can relate positively to negative humor forms (cynicism, sarcasm). Distinguish sadness (may impair capability) from ill-humor (may be antagonistic).

rubrics_metrics.name: State cheerfulness components
rubrics_metrics.description: State cheerfulness components include presence of a cheerful mood (more tranquil/composed) and presence of a merry/hilarity state (more shallow/outward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State cheerfulness differs from exhilaration in duration and stimulus-independence; assess via state STCI items sensitive to momentary mood and via elicitations that vary situationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: State seriousness components
rubrics_metrics.description: State seriousness components include earnestness (task-oriented attitude), pensiveness (thoughtful mood), and soberness (dispassionate frame of mind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State seriousness captures transient teleic/goal-oriented frames that reduce receptivity to certain humor types; include measures that index cognitive framing and appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: State bad mood components
rubrics_metrics.description: State bad mood components include sadness/melancholy (presence of sad mood) and ill-humor (presence of grumpy/grouchy mood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate transient sadness from ill-humored antagonism when predicting humor appreciation/production and social responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facet-level operationalization and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each trait (cheerfulness, seriousness, bad mood) was operationalized via multiple definitional facets (5, 6, and 5 respectively) and item pools to capture prevalence, elicitors, behavior, and attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing instruments, generate facets to cover prevalence, intensity, duration, and situational behavior; ensure items sample both affective and mental/attitudinal aspects. Use facet-level analyses to examine differential relationships with humor outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: State–trait relationship parameters: threshold, intensity, duration, robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Key parameters linking traits to states are ease of entering a state (threshold in), intensity of experienced state, duration, and resistance to being brought out of a state (robustness/threshold out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess these parameters by asking respondents to rate how easily they enter a state, how intense it is, how long it lasts, and how much it takes to remove them. Use these to test hypotheses about traits predicting state dynamics (e.g., trait cheerfulness -> low threshold in, high robustness).

rubrics_metrics.name: STCI measurement instruments and psychometric criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: State–Trait-Cheerfulness Inventory (STCI) versions: STCI-T<106> (component form), STCI-T<60> (standard trait), STCI-S<30> (standard state). Peer-evaluation (he/she) forms and modified state instructions for longer time spans were developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha; reported .86–.96 for STCI-T<106>, .80–.94 for STCI-T<60>; .85–.94 for STCI-S), test–retest reliability (.73–.86 for trait forms; lower for state forms), and sensitivity of items for mood change. Use peer versions to validate self-report and consider short/standard forms depending on study constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping (or losing) humor under adversity — experimental criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Keeping humor" operationalized as minimal pre-post change in STCI-S cheerfulness and minimal increase in STCI-S bad mood following an adverse induction; "losing humor" as decline in state cheerfulness and increase in bad mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unobtrusive, moderately intense mood induction (e.g., room manipulations, scenarios) and pre/post STCI-S measurements. Classify individuals (e.g., median split or extreme groups) on cheerful composure facet (CH3) to test moderation hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait cheerfulness as disposition for exhilaration and humor initiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Trait cheerfulness predicts greater facility for exhilaration (smiling, laughter, affective responses) and a greater tendency to initiate/entertain in social situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure facial/expression behavior (e.g., FACS coding), self-report state changes after humorous stimuli, and behavioral indices of initiation. Expect trait cheerfulness to predict frequency, intensity, and duration of amusement responses and post-stimulus mood improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait seriousness and preferences in humor appreciation and creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Trait seriousness relates to interest in humor, preferences across humor types (e.g., incongruity-resolution vs nonsense), and to humor-creation processes; semi-serious individuals may prefer certain structured humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for linear and non-linear (inverted-U) relationships between seriousness and funniness ratings across humor types. Use canonical/regression analyses linking seriousness facets to multiple humor appreciation and creation variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait bad mood as distinct form of humorlessness and predictor of negative humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad mood is a distinct affective form of humorlessness that may impair generation of positive affect and may facilitate preference for or production of negative/misanthropic humor (sarcasm, cynicism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate facets (sadness vs ill-humor) in predictions: sadness may reduce capacity for humor even if desired, ill-humor may produce antagonistic humor. Include measures of aversiveness and preference for negative humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blends of cheerfulness and seriousness predict forms of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations of high/low cheerfulness and high/low seriousness yield different humor styles — e.g., high cheerfulness/low seriousness enjoy slapstick and shallow comedy; high cheerfulness/high seriousness smile benevolently and prefer contemplative humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model interactions between cheerfulness and seriousness to predict type of humor appreciated or produced; consider typologies (e.g., Raskin types) when designing stimuli sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of traits as moderator variables and experimental manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological recommendation to use the three traits as moderator variables in experiments and to experimentally manipulate states (cheerfulness, seriousness, bad mood) to test causal effects on humor responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with mood-inducing rooms/scenarios, facial-feedback manipulations, or situational tasks, and test trait × situation interactions. Use modified STCI-S instructions (last week/month/year) to assess longer-lasting states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item selection sensitivity and state scale construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing the state scale (STCI-S<30>), items were selected for sensitivity to mood alterations; state scales should be sensitive to situational change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select items that show variability with mood inductions, check internal consistency and test–retest, and consider shorter/standard forms depending on experimental constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent validity with existing sense-of-humor scales and factor structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect trait cheerfulness to load with traditional sense-of-humor scales forming a social-affective axis, while seriousness and bad mood form separate (mental/negative) axes in joint factor analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use joint factor analyses of STCI facets with other humor inventories to establish shared factor space; interpret cheerfulness as social-affective dimension and seriousness/bad mood as separate dimensions influencing distinct humor components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality correlates as validation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheerfulness correlates positively with Extraversion/Energy, Agreeableness/Friendliness, and Emotional Stability (low Neuroticism); bad mood correlates with Neuroticism and disagreeableness; seriousness correlates with introversion/conscientiousness patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established personality inventories (EPQ-R, NEOPI-R, BFQ) to validate STCI constructs and to interpret their nomological networks when relating temperament to humor-related behaviors.
